newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right leader urges vote against Juppe.
newsitem.headline: French far-right leader urges vote against Juppe.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen urged supporters of his National Front on Thursday to go all out to defeat outgoing conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Juppe, who is seeking a National Assembly seat from a constituency in Bordeaux, the southwestern city where he also serves as mayor, "is the archetype of the most unjust and ferocious enemy of the National Front", Le Pen told a campaign rally in the French capital.

Juppe, who announced this week he would step down after Sunday's election no matter who won, has had strong words for Le Pen in the past and has consistently ruled out making political deals with the Front.
Last year, he called le Pen "deeply, almost viscerally racist, antisemitic and xenophobic".

Le Pen also urged defeat for conservative Paris mayor Jean Tiberi, conservative Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, centrist Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy, Communist Party leader Robert Hue and Socialist Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann, who led an anti-Front mass march in her eastern city.
Juppe stepped down after the governing centre-right suffered a surprise defeat in last Sunday's first-round vote.

He said he was accepting the blame for a major upset following President Jacques Chirac's call for an early election, intended to give France a "new elan" and a renewed majority for the next five years, during the shift to a single European currency.
Le Pen's call for Juppe's defeat was surprising only because of its strong language.

Le Pen has portrayed the Front as a king-maker in Sunday's parliamentary election runoff, saying it would support only candidates who endorsed its anti-European stance and its plan to reserve jobs, housing, education, health care and welfare for native-born French citizens.
The Front scored its best parliamentary election result in the first-round ballot on Sunday, and analysts said its voters could play a key role in determining whether the left or right would govern.
The Front boasted that its candidates would be standing in a high 132 of France's 577 constituencies in the second round.

Official Interior Ministry results gave the Front a national first-round score of 14.9 percent, only slightly less than the record 15 percent Le Pen won in the 1995 presidential election and significantly better than its 12.4 percent score in the last general election in 1993.
